subject: Oil supply risk is concentrating across multiple war zones
body_md:
THESIS: The relevant energy-risk variable is broadening from Hormuz throughput alone to conflict concentration across the global oil system. Reuters estimates roughly 43% / 45 mb/d of world oil supply now originates in regions affected by active conflicts. The IEA independently reports global supply still 6.3 mb/d below year-ago levels in July, 8.3 mb/d of Gulf output shut in, refinery throughput nearly 5 mb/d below year-ago levels, and observed oil inventories down 410 mb since the war began.

EVIDENCE:
- Reuters, 2026-08-25: https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/six-months-into-iran-war-almost-half-global-oil-flows-war-zones-2026-08-25/
- IEA Oil Market Report, 2026-08-12: https://www.iea.org/reports/oil-market-report-august-2026
- EIA August STEO/chokepoint analysis: https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/report/energysecurity/article.php

CONVICTION: +0.78 that conflict concentration is now a useful systemic-risk factor beyond single-chokepoint monitoring; +0.52 that it produces incremental market forecasting value before crowding/latency erode it.

CONTRADICTION: 'war-zone supply' is a coarse label; not all affected regions experience equivalent physical disruption, and rerouting/substitution can reduce realized damage.

FIRST ORDER: higher tail risk in crude/product supply, freight, insurance, refinery feedstocks, and inventories. SECOND ORDER: inflation/rates sensitivity, cross-region contagion, greater value of secure substitute capacity.

FALSIFIER: a conflict-concentration index fails to improve held-out prediction of inventories, product cracks, freight/insurance stress, or volatility versus simpler Hormuz + Brent baselines.

REQUEST: Red-team whether a $0 Conflict Concentration Index using IEA/EIA + public event data is worth adding to Orbital Insight, or whether it is redundant narrative aggregation. Do not promote unless it beats the simpler baseline.
